title: High priest John kills his brother Jesus in the Temple; Bagoses defiles it
note: Johanan (John) murdered his brother Jesus in the Temple; the Persian general Bagoses entered the sanctuary and laid a tax on every daily sacrifice for seven years. Josephus: "under 'another Artaxerxes' (Artaxerxes II); no year given".

title: Manasseh, brother of Jaddua, marries Sanballat's daughter
note: The elders forced Manasseh to choose between his foreign wife Nikaso and the altar; he went over to his father-in-law Sanballat, who promised him a temple of his own. Josephus: "in the days of Darius III, before Alexander's invasion".

title: Alexander the Great at Jerusalem bows before the high priest Jaddua
note: Jaddua went out to Sapha (Mount Scopus) in his robes; Alexander bowed to the Name on his mitre, sacrificed in the Temple, was shown Daniel's prophecy of a Greek conqueror, and let the Jews keep their laws. Josephus: "after the siege of Tyre and the taking of Gaza".

title: Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim built for Manasseh
note: Sanballat built a temple like Jerusalem's on Gerizim and made Manasseh its high priest, the beginning of the separate Samaritan cult centre. Josephus: "Alexander 'permitted Sanballat ... to build' it during the siege of Tyre".

title: Ptolemy I takes Jerusalem on a Sabbath
note: Ptolemy son of Lagus entered on the Sabbath when the Jews would not fight, and carried many captives to Egypt; Josephus cites Agatharchides mocking the Jews for this. Josephus: "'he came into the city on a sabbath day, as if he would offer sacrifices'".

title: Hezekiah the high priest goes to Egypt after the battle of Gaza
note: Hecataeus says Hezekiah, a Jewish chief priest about 66 years old, followed Ptolemy I to Egypt with many Jews; it shows the Jewish community in Egypt under the first Ptolemy. Josephus: "battle of Gaza 'in the eleventh year after the death of Alexander, and in the hundred and seventeenth olympiad'".

title: Simon the Just becomes high priest
note: Remembered for his piety and kindness to his people; the Mishnah names him one of the last of the Great Assembly. Josephus: "'When Onias the high priest was dead, his son Simon became his successor. He was called Simon the Just'".

title: Seventy-two elders translate the Law into Greek for Ptolemy II
note: At Demetrius of Phalerum's suggestion Ptolemy freed about 120,000 Jewish captives and asked Eleazar for six elders from each tribe, who translated the Law on the island of Pharos; this became the Septuagint. Josephus: "under Ptolemy Philadelphus, Eleazar being high priest; finished 'in seventy-two days'".

title: Ptolemy III Euergetes sacrifices at the Jerusalem Temple
note: Instead of thanking Egypt's gods, the king came to Jerusalem and offered many sacrifices according to Jewish law. Josephus: "after he 'had gotten possession of all Syria by force'".

title: Joseph son of Tobias wins the tax farm of Syria and Judea
note: Joseph outbid the Syrian cities and collected the taxes for 22 years, making the Tobiad family the richest and most Hellenized house in Judea. Josephus: "when Onias II refused tribute to 'Ptolemy Euergetes'; held it 22 years".

title: Antiochus III settles 2,000 Jewish families from Babylonia in Lydia and Phrygia
note: The king moved loyal Jewish families from Mesopotamia to garrison rebellious Lydia and Phrygia, with land and ten years' tax relief; the start of the Jewish diaspora of Asia Minor. Josephus: "letter of Antiochus to Zeuxis, written when he 'was in the superior provinces'".

title: Antiochus III takes Judea and issues a charter for the Temple
note: The Jews welcomed Antiochus; he granted Temple supplies, tax relief for the elders, priests and scribes, and forbade foreigners and unclean animals in the Temple. Josephus: "after Scopas was defeated at Panium".

title: Hyrcanus the Tobiad kills himself as Antiochus IV takes the throne
note: Hyrcanus built the fortified palace at Tyros (Iraq al-Amir, still standing) and killed himself fearing Antiochus. Josephus: "he ruled beyond Jordan seven years, all the time Seleucus reigned; died when Antiochus Epiphanes became king".

title: Jason and Menelaus buy the high priesthood; gymnasium built in Jerusalem
note: Jason, then Menelaus, obtained the office from Antiochus; the Hellenizers built a gymnasium and hid their circumcision, the start of the crisis behind the Maccabean revolt. Josephus: "'upon the death of Onias ... they gave the high priesthood to Jesus his brother' (who called himself Jason)".

note: Antiochus entered without a fight, killed many of the opposing party and carried off the Temple's golden altar, lampstand and table. Josephus: "'in the hundred and forty-third year of the kingdom of the Seleucidae'".

note: The Jews began dating documents by Simon's years, the start of Hasmonean independence. Josephus: "'after a hundred and seventy years of the kingdom of the Assyrians ... in their public records, they wrote, in the first year of Simon the benefactor and ethnarch'".

note: The Seleucid garrison fortress that had dominated the Temple was demolished and its hill levelled. Josephus: "'which cost them three whole years'".

note: The Idumeans could stay if they were circumcised and kept the Jewish law; Herod's family came from these converts. Josephus: "with the taking of Dora (Adora) and Marissa".

title: John Hyrcanus destroys the Samaritan temple on Gerizim
note: Hyrcanus took Shechem and Gerizim and destroyed the temple that Alexander had allowed. Josephus: "'which temple was now deserted two hundred years after it was built'".

title: Hyrcanus breaks with the Pharisees and joins the Sadducees
note: Eleazar told him to give up the high priesthood because his mother had been a captive; Hyrcanus repealed Pharisaic ordinances, starting the long Pharisee–Hasmonean feud. Josephus: "late in his reign, after Eleazar's insult at a feast".

note: While offering incense alone, Hyrcanus heard that his sons had just beaten Antiochus Cyzicenus, and it proved true; Samaria was razed. Josephus: "siege of one year; 'on the very same day on which his sons fought with Antiochus Cyzicenus'". Hyrcanus's sons Aristobulus and Antigonus besieged Samaria, beat Antiochus Cyzicenus, and razed the city.

title: Death of John Hyrcanus after 31 years
note: Josephus says God judged him worthy of three privileges: rule of the nation, the high priesthood and prophecy. Josephus: "'administered the government in the best manner for thirty-one years, and then died'". Josephus calls Hyrcanus the one man who held rule, high priesthood and the gift of prophecy together.

title: Aristobulus I becomes the first Hasmonean to wear a crown
note: He turned the high priesthood into a monarchy, imprisoned his mother and three brothers, and let her starve. Josephus: "'first of all put a diadem on his head, four hundred eighty and one years and three months after the people had been delivered from the Babylonish slavery'". Aristobulus turned the high-priestly rule into a kingdom, jailed his brothers and starved his mother.

title: Judas the Essene's prophecy fulfilled: Antigonus killed at Strato's Tower
note: Judas, an Essene who 'had never failed' in his predictions, foretold Antigonus's death at 'Strato's Tower'; Antigonus was killed in an underground passage of that name in Jerusalem. note: He forced the Ituraeans of Galilee to be circumcised and died in remorse, vomiting blood. Josephus: "'when he had reigned one year'".

note: Salome Alexandra, Aristobulus's widow, freed the brothers and made Jannaeus king and high priest (and, most think, married him). Josephus: "after Aristobulus's death".

note: Treachery opened the city and Jannaeus's men sacked it. Josephus: "after a year's siege".

note: The nation rose against Jannaeus at a feast and his mercenaries killed more than 6,000; Antiquities says it was Tabernacles. A six-year civil war followed. Josephus: "“at a festival; for at those feasts seditions are generally begun”".

note: The crowd's love for him at Tabernacles alarmed Herod, whose men held him under water in the palace pools 'in sport'. Josephus: "'upon the approach of the feast of tabernacles ... When therefore the festival was over, and he was feasting at Jericho'". He was 17 and had served one year (35 BC). Month taken as Tishri, just after the feast. title: Great earthquake in Judea in Herod's seventh year
note: About 10,000 people and many cattle died. Archaeologists (de Vaux) linked cracked cisterns and destruction at Khirbet Qumran to this quake. Josephus: "'in the seventh year of the reign of Herod ... there was an earthquake in Judea, such a one as had not happened at any other time'; Actium 'fell into the hundred eighty and seventh olympiad'". The quake killed many cattle and about 30,000 people, but not Herod's army camped in the open.

title: Herod executes the aged Hyrcanus II
note: Accused of plotting with the Nabatean king Malchus, the last surviving Hasmonean ruler was put to death. Josephus: "before Herod went to meet Octavian; Hyrcanus 'above fourscore years old'".

title: Octavian confirms Herod as king at Rhodes
note: Herod laid aside his diadem and spoke frankly of his loyalty to Antony; Octavian restored it and later added Jericho, Gaza, Joppa and Strato's Tower. Josephus: "after Actium". Herod came without his diadem, admitted his loyalty to Antony, and was crowned again by Octavian.

title: Herod has Queen Mariamne executed
note: Falsely accused by Salome, Mariamne went to her death calmly; Herod, half-mad with grief, fell ill. Josephus: "after his return from Octavian".

title: Herod institutes games for Augustus in Jerusalem
note: Trophies in the theatre, thought to be images, caused outrage and a failed plot by ten citizens to kill Herod. Josephus: "quinquennial games with theatre and amphitheatre".

title: Herod refounds Samaria as Sebaste
note: Settled with 6,000 colonists and given a temple to Augustus; Herod married Malthace and here later strangled two sons. Josephus: "named for Augustus (Sebastos)". Herod settled 6,000 colonists in the city and built a temple to Augustus.

title: Famine in Herod's thirteenth year; Herod buys Egyptian grain
note: Drought and plague; Herod melted his palace gold and silver to buy grain from Petronius, prefect of Egypt. Josephus: "'on this very year, which was the thirteenth year of the reign of Herod, very great calamities came upon the country'".

title: Herod begins rebuilding the Temple (15th year)
note: Herod doubled the Temple enclosure, built new cloisters and rebuilt the fortress Antonia. War's 15th year differs from the 18th year in Antiquities 15.11.1. Josephus: "“in the fifteenth year of his reign, Herod rebuilt the temple”".

title: Herod makes Simon son of Boethus high priest and marries Mariamne II
note: The Boethus family, from Alexandria, held the office often afterwards and is linked by many to the Boethusians of rabbinic tradition. Josephus: "to raise his bride's family".

title: Herod begins Caesarea Maritima at Strato's Tower
note: Herod built a harbour, Sebastos, larger than Piraeus, with a temple of Augustus and Rome. Josephus: "'this city was thus finished in twelve years'".

title: Herod excuses the Essenes from the oath of loyalty
note: Herod demanded an oath of loyalty but excused Pollio, Sameas and the Essenes, whom Josephus likens to Pythagoreans, out of respect for Menahem. Josephus: "Herod 'had these Essens in such honor'; context of his 17th–18th year".

title: Herod begins rebuilding the Temple in his 18th year
note: He trained 1,000 priests as masons and enlarged the Temple Mount; work went on until AD 63/64 (John 2:20, 'forty and six years'). Josephus: "'Herod, in the eighteenth year of his reign ... undertook a very great work, that is, to build of himself the temple of God'".

title: Herod's sanctuary finished; dedication falls on his accession day
note: Herod sacrificed 300 oxen; the porticoes took eight years. Josephus adds a tradition that rain fell only at night while the Temple was being built. Josephus: "'the temple itself was built by the priests in a year and six months ... at the same time with this celebration ... fell also the day of the king's inauguration'".

title: Marcus Agrippa sacrifices a hecatomb at the Jerusalem Temple
note: Augustus's right-hand man feasted the people and sacrificed in the Temple; the next year he confirmed the rights of the Ionian Jews. Josephus: "visit to Herod's kingdom".

title: Caesarea dedicated in Herod's 28th year, Olympiad 192
note: Games for Augustus were held with gladiators and wild beasts, to recur every fifth year. Josephus: "'The entire building being accomplished: in the tenth year, the solemnity of it fell into the twenty-eighth year of Herod's reign, and into the hundred and ninety-second olympiad'". Herod rebuilt Strato's Tower as Caesarea with a harbour bigger than the Piraeus, and founded five-yearly games for Caesar.

title: Herod robs David's tomb; two guards killed by a flame
note: Herod took gold furniture by night; when his guards went deeper a flame burst out and killed two. In fear he built a white-marble monument at the entrance. Josephus: "after Hyrcanus had opened it before him".

title: Herod's sons Alexander and Aristobulus strangled at Sebaste
note: Mariamne's sons, condemned by a council under Saturninus, were strangled and buried at Alexandreion. Josephus: "after the trial at Berytus". Mariamne's two sons were executed on Herod's order after a hearing at Berytus, and buried at Alexandrium.

title: Over 6,000 Pharisees refuse the oath to Augustus and Herod
note: Pheroras's wife paid their fine; they foretold that Herod's line would lose the throne, and Herod killed several of them. Josephus: "'these very men did not swear, being above six thousand'".

title: Joseph son of Ellemus serves as high priest for one day: "the fast"
note: Matthias the high priest became ritually unclean in a dream the night before, so his relative Joseph officiated that day only; the only such case Josephus records. Josephus: "'there was another person made high priest for a single day, that very day which the Jews observed as a fast'". The fast is the Day of Atonement (10 Tishri) before Herod's death, most often taken as 5 BC; the eclipse that follows in the text is a separate night in spring. title: Golden eagle torn down; Matthias burned alive the night of the eclipse
note: Students of the teachers Judas and Matthias cut down Herod's golden eagle from the Temple gate; Herod had Matthias and others burned alive that night and deposed the high priest Matthias. Josephus: "'that very night there was an eclipse of the moon'". The eclipse is usually taken as 13 March 4 BC (already in the app), which fell at full moon in Adar (II) of that year. title: Archelaus's troops kill 3,000 at Passover
note: Mourners demanding punishment for Herod's executions filled the Temple; Archelaus's cavalry killed 3,000 and the feast was abandoned. Josephus: "'upon the approach of that feast of unleavened bread ... which feast is called the Passover'". Passover of 4 BC, just after Herod's death; day taken as 14 Nisan. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed. Mourners for the men Herod burned rioted.

title: Pentecost revolt against Sabinus; Temple porticoes burned
note: Pilgrims besieged the Roman procurator Sabinus; the Romans burned the porticoes and looted 400 talents from the Temple treasury. Josephus: "'on the approach of pentecost, which is a festival of ours, so called from the days of our forefathers, a great many ten thousands of men got together'". Pentecost 4 BC (early Sivan). Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed. Pilgrims besieged the procurator Sabinus.

title: Students cut down Herod's golden eagle from the Temple gate
note: Followers of the teachers Judas and Matthias cut down the eagle. Herod had the teachers and the young men who did it burned alive. Antiquities ties this to the eclipse already in the app. Josephus: "when “a rumor was spread abroad that the king was dying”; done “at midday”".

title: Death of Herod the Great at Jericho
note: After a terrible illness and the execution of Antipater, Herod died and was carried in state to the Herodium; his will divided the kingdom among three sons. Placed in 4 BC, the usual date (after the lunar eclipse Josephus mentions). Those who date Jesus’ birth to 2 BC, as Ken Johnson does, put Herod’s death in 1 BC, after the eclipse of 10 January 1 BC. Josephus: "'he died, the fifth day after he had caused Antipater to be slain; having reigned, since he had procured Antigonus to be slain, thirty-four years; but since he had been declared king by the Romans, thirty-seven'". Herod died at Jericho and was carried 200 furlongs to Herodium for burial.

title: Judas son of Hezekiah, Simon and Athronges claim kingship
note: Judas seized the arsenal at Sepphoris, Herod's slave Simon burned Jericho palace, and the shepherd Athronges wore a crown; 'Judea was full of robberies'. Josephus: "the disturbances after Herod's death".

title: Varus crucifies 2,000 rebels
note: The governor of Syria burned Sepphoris and Emmaus and crushed the revolt. Josephus: "'the number of those that were crucified on this account were two thousand'". The Syrian legate Varus burned Sepphoris and Emmaus and crucified 2,000 rebels around Jerusalem.

title: Augustus divides Herod's kingdom among Archelaus, Antipas and Philip
note: Archelaus became ethnarch of Judea, Samaria and Idumea; Antipas tetrarch of Galilee and Perea; Philip tetrarch of Batanea, Trachonitis and Auranitis. Josephus: "after hearing the delegations at Rome". Archelaus received half the kingdom as ethnarch; Antipas got Galilee and Perea, and Philip Batanea and Trachonitis.

title: Archelaus banished to Vienne; Judea becomes a Roman province
note: After complaints from Jews and Samaritans, Augustus deposed Archelaus. Judea came under the procurator Coponius. Josephus: "“in the ninth year of his government he was banished to Vienna, a city of Gaul”".

title: Simon the Essene interprets Archelaus's dream; Archelaus banished
note: Archelaus dreamed of ten ears of corn eaten by oxen; Simon, 'of the sect of the Essens', said his ten-year rule was at an end. Five days later Augustus summoned him, and he was banished to Vienne. Josephus: "'in the tenth year of Archelaus's government'; the summons came five days after the dream". Simon read the nine ears as nine years of rule and the oxen as a change of fortune.

title: Census of Quirinius; Judas the Galilean founds the "fourth philosophy"
note: When Judea became a Roman province, Judas of Gamala and the Pharisee Saddok urged refusal of the tax as slavery, founding the movement Josephus blames for the war. Coponius was the first prefect. Josephus: "'the taxings ... which were made in the thirty-seventh year of Caesar's victory over Antony at Actium'". Judas called it cowardice to pay tribute and accept mortal masters after God.

title: Quirinius appoints Ananus (Annas) son of Seth high priest
note: The Annas of the Gospels; five of his sons later held the office, which Josephus calls unique. Josephus: "after Joazar was deprived".

title: Josephus describes the Essenes (Antiquities 18)
note: About 4,000 men who held property in common, did not marry or keep slaves, sent offerings to the Temple but sacrificed apart, and chose priests to prepare their food; he likens them to the Dacian Polistae. Josephus: "in his account of the sects at the time of the census".

title: Samaritans scatter human bones in the Temple at Passover
note: Samaritans slipped in at night and defiled the porticoes, after which the Jews barred them. Josephus: "under Coponius, 'as the Jews were celebrating the feast of unleavened bread ... the priests ... open the temple-gates just after midnight'". Coponius governed AD 6–9; year uncertain (taken as AD 7). Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.

title: Death of Augustus; Tiberius succeeds
note: Josephus reports the succession; Philip and Antipas kept their tetrarchies. Josephus: "Augustus “had reigned fifty-seven years, six months, and two days”". Julian date from Roman sources (Suetonius); Josephus gives only the length of the reign.

title: Valerius Gratus appoints Joseph Caiaphas high priest
note: Caiaphas, son-in-law of Annas, held office about 18 years and presided at the trial of Jesus. Josephus: "after Ishmael, Eleazar and Simon each held it about a year".

title: Tiberius expels the Jews from Rome; 4,000 sent to Sardinia
note: Four Jewish swindlers took Fulvia's gifts for the Temple; Tiberius drafted 4,000 Jews for Sardinia. Josephus: "after the fraud on Fulvia".

title: Herod Antipas founds Tiberias
note: Built on a graveyard, so observant Jews thought it unclean; Antipas forced settlers to live there. Josephus: "named for Tiberius". Philip built Caesarea at the springs of the Jordan (Paneas) and Julias; Antipas built Tiberias in Galilee and another Julias in Perea.

title: Pilate brings Caesar's images into Jerusalem
note: Crowds lay at Caesarea for five days and bared their necks to the swords; Pilate gave in and removed the standards. Josephus: "when he 'removed the army from Caesarea to Jerusalem, to take their winter quarters there'". Crowds lay before Pilate's house at Caesarea for five days and nights.

title: Pilate builds an aqueduct with Temple money; protesters clubbed
note: Disguised soldiers beat the protesting crowd with clubs, killing many. Josephus: "'Pilate undertook to bring a current of water to Jerusalem, and did it with the sacred money'".

title: Pilate spends the Temple treasure (Corban) on an aqueduct
note: Soldiers disguised in the crowd beat the protesters at his tribunal, and many died. Josephus: "“After this he raised another disturbance, by expending that sacred treasure which is called Corban upon aqueducts”".

title: Herod Antipas executes John the Baptist at Machaerus
note: Josephus says John was a good man who urged virtue and baptism, and that Antipas killed him fearing a rising; many Jews saw Antipas's defeat as God's punishment. Josephus gives no year; placed about AD 31, before the cross in AD 32. Josephus: "no date; told as the cause of Antipas's defeat by Aretas (AD 36)".

title: Death of Philip the tetrarch in Tiberius's 20th year
note: A just and quiet ruler, buried in the tomb he had built; his territory went to the province of Syria. Josephus: "'in the twentieth year of the reign of Tiberius, after he had been tetrarch ... thirty-seven years'".

title: Vitellius at Passover returns the high priest's robes and removes Caiaphas
note: Vitellius gave the Jews custody of the vestments worn 'at the three yearly festivals, and on the fast day' and replaced Caiaphas with Jonathan son of Annas. Josephus: "'it was at the time of that festival which is called the Passover'". Usually Passover AD 36 (some argue AD 37). Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.

title: King Aretas IV defeats Herod Antipas
note: Antipas's army was destroyed; Tiberius ordered Vitellius to make war on Aretas. Josephus: "over Antipas's divorce of Aretas's daughter to marry Herodias".

title: Pilate attacks the Samaritans gathered at Tirathaba
note: Pilate's cavalry killed many and executed the leaders; the Samaritans complained to Vitellius, which ended Pilate's career. Josephus: "a man promised to show 'those sacred vessels which were laid under that place, because Moses put them there'".

title: Pilate sent to Rome after ten years in Judea
note: Vitellius sent Marcellus to take over and ordered Pilate to answer to the emperor. Josephus: "'Pilate, when he had tarried ten years in Judea, made haste to Rome ... but before he could get to Rome Tiberius was dead'".

title: Tiberius dies; Gaius frees Agrippa and makes him king
note: Agrippa, jailed six months for wishing Gaius emperor, was released and given Philip's tetrarchy with the title of king. Josephus: "“until Tiberius died, after he had reigned twenty-two years, six months, and three days”". Julian date of Tiberius's death from Roman sources (Tacitus, Suetonius). Gaius gave Agrippa a gold chain as heavy as his iron one, Philip's tetrarchy and the title of king.

title: At a Jerusalem festival Vitellius learns of Tiberius's death
note: Vitellius replaced Jonathan with his brother Theophilus, had the people swear allegiance to Gaius, and called off the war on Aretas. Josephus: "'an ancient festival of the Jews being then just approaching ... on the fourth day letters came to him, which informed him of the death of Tiberius'".

title: Josephus born in Jerusalem
note: Born to a priestly family of the first course with Hasmonean descent on his mother's side. Josephus: "'I was born to Matthias in the first year of the reign of Caius Caesar'".

title: Herod Antipas and Herodias banished to Gaul
note: Accused by Agrippa of stockpiling arms, Antipas lost his tetrarchy; Herodias chose to share his exile. Josephus: "Gaius 'appointed Lyons, a city of Gaul, to be his place of habitation'". Pushed by Herodias to seek a crown, Antipas was accused by Agrippa and exiled by Gaius.

title: Philo leads the Alexandrian Jewish embassy to Caligula
note: Gaius refused to hear Philo, who told his companions that the emperor had set God against himself. Josephus: "after the 'tumult ... at Alexandria'; Apion spoke for the Greeks".

title: Caligula orders his statue set up in the Temple; Jews refuse to sow
note: Tens of thousands begged Petronius to kill them first; he risked death by delaying, Agrippa persuaded Gaius to withdraw the order, and Gaius's death in January 41 saved Petronius. Josephus: "'they continued firm ... and left off the tilling of their ground ... while the season of the year required them to sow it'". Jews massed before Petronius rather than allow the statue.

title: Some 50,000 Jews massacred at Seleucia
note: After the Jewish robber-princes Asineus and Anileus fell, Jews fled to Seleucia, where Greeks and Syrians killed more than 50,000. Josephus: "after the fall of Asineus and Anileus".

title: Gaius (Caligula) assassinated; Claudius made emperor
note: Agrippa I helped negotiate between Claudius and the Senate. Josephus: "“when Caius had reigned three years and eight months, and had been slain by treachery”". Julian date from Roman sources; Josephus gives the length of the reign.

title: Claudius gives Agrippa I Judea and Samaria
note: Agrippa, who had helped Claudius to the throne, now ruled the whole of Herod's kingdom; Claudius also issued an edict for the Alexandrian Jews. Josephus: "on Claudius's accession". Claudius added Judea, Samaria and the kingdom of Lysanias, and gave Chalcis to Agrippa's brother Herod.

title: Agrippa I begins the Third Wall of Jerusalem
note: Built to enclose the new northern suburb (Bezetha); it would have made the city impregnable, Josephus says, had it been finished. Josephus: "Claudius, warned by Marsus, ordered it stopped". Josephus says the wall would have made the city impregnable had it been finished; Agrippa's death stopped the work.

title: Young men of Dora set Caesar's statue in the synagogue
note: Agrippa protested and Petronius ordered the offenders arrested, upholding the Jews' right to their synagogue. Josephus: "Petronius's edict quotes Claudius's recent decree".

title: Agrippa I struck down at Caesarea during the games for Caesar
note: When flatterers hailed him as a god he did not rebuke them, saw the owl again, and died of pains in his belly; compare Acts 12:20–23. Josephus: "'when Agrippa had reigned three years over all Judea'; 'on the second day of which shows he put on a garment made wholly of silver'; died after five days, 'in the fifty-fourth year of his age, and in the seventh year of his reign'". Judea returned to procurators (Cuspius Fadus, then Tiberius Alexander).

title: Claudius lets the Jews keep the high priest's vestments
note: Fadus and Longinus had demanded the robes be kept in Antonia; the young Agrippa (II) won Claudius's consent that they stay with the Jews. Josephus: "'This letter is dated before the fourth of the calends of July, when Ruffis and Pompeius Sylvanus are consuls'". a.d. IV Kal. Iul. = 28 June; the suffect consuls Rufus and Pompeius Silvanus place it in AD 45. Roman calendar = Julian by then. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed.

title: Herod of Chalcis given power over the Temple and high priests
note: Herod king of Chalcis and his heirs could appoint high priests and manage the Temple treasury. Josephus: "by Claudius after the vestments dispute".

title: Theudas leads followers to the Jordan; beheaded by Fadus
note: Claiming to be a prophet who would part the Jordan, he led a crowd with their goods; cavalry killed many, and his head was taken to Jerusalem. Josephus: "'while Fadus was procurator of Judea'".

title: Great famine in Judea; Queen Helena of Adiabene brings food
note: Helena, a convert to Judaism, bought grain in Alexandria and figs from Cyprus, and her son Izates sent money. Josephus: "'Under these procurators [Fadus and Tiberius Alexander] that great famine happened in Judea, in which queen Helena bought corn in Egypt'".

title: Tiberius Alexander crucifies James and Simon, sons of Judas the Galilean
note: The founder's sons kept his movement alive; Tiberius Alexander, an apostate nephew of Philo, had them crucified. Josephus: "'the sons of Judas of Galilee were now slain'".

title: A Roman soldier's insult at Passover ends in a deadly crush
note: Stones were thrown, Cumanus brought in troops, and in the panic in the narrow passages about 20,000 died (Jewish War says 30,000). Josephus: "'on the fourth day of the feast, a certain soldier let down his breeches, and exposed his privy members to the multitude'". Cumanus governed AD 48–52; usually dated AD 49 (year not given). 4th day of Unleavened Bread = 18 Nisan. Computed: first visible crescent after astronomical new moon (Astronomy Engine), Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1 day, and ±1 month if that year's intercalation differed. A soldier on the Temple cloister exposed himself to the crowd.

title: A soldier tears up a Torah scroll; Cumanus beheads him
note: To calm the outcry Cumanus had the soldier executed. Josephus: "after the robbery of Caesar's slave Stephanus". After a robbery on the road, a soldier destroyed a Torah scroll in a village raid.

title: Galilean pilgrim killed at Geman on the way to Tabernacles
note: The killing led to Jewish–Samaritan fighting. Quadratus investigated, and Claudius banished Cumanus and had the tribune Celer executed in Jerusalem. Josephus: "“as a great number of Jews were going up to Jerusalem to the feast [of tabernacles]”". Tabernacles (Tishri); about AD 51/52. Jewish reprisals, Cumanus's bribery and Quadratus's inquiry led Claudius, persuaded by young Agrippa, to execute Samaritan leaders and banish Cumanus.

title: Felix, brother of Pallas, made procurator of Judea
note: Felix later married Drusilla, Agrippa II's sister, and heard Paul (Acts 24). Josephus: "after Cumanus".

title: Claudius gives Agrippa II the tetrarchy of Philip in his twelfth year
note: Agrippa II lost Chalcis but gained a larger kingdom; he ruled until the end of the century. Josephus: "'when he had already completed the twelfth year of his reign, he bestowed upon Agrippa the tetrarchy of Philip and Batanea'".

title: Josephus tries the three sects and lives three years with Banus
note: Josephus says he went through the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes, then lived with the ascetic Banus in the desert, wearing what grew on trees and bathing often in cold water. Josephus: "'when I was about sixteen years old ... Banus ... lived in the desert'; returned 'in the nineteenth year of my age' and followed the Pharisees".

title: Claudius dies; Nero succeeds
note: Josephus notes the adoption of Nero through Agrippina. Felix was procurator, and Agrippa II was given Philip's former tetrarchy. Josephus: "“Claudius… when he had administered the government thirteen years, eight months, and twenty days, died”". Julian date from Roman sources.

title: Helena and Izates buried in pyramids near Jerusalem
note: Their bones were laid in three pyramids three furlongs from the city, usually identified with the 'Tomb of the Kings'. Josephus: "Izates 'died ... when he had reigned twenty-four years'; Helena soon after".

title: The sicarii murder the former high priest Jonathan
note: Jonathan son of Annas criticised Felix, who had the sicarii stab him; their daggers in festival crowds began a run of killings. Josephus: "on Felix's prompting". The Sicarii hid daggers under their clothes and killed people in festival crowds; after Jonathan, many were killed every day.

title: The "Egyptian" prophet leads a crowd to the Mount of Olives
note: Felix killed 400 and took 200 prisoners; the Egyptian escaped and was never seen again. Josephus: "promised the walls of Jerusalem would fall at his command". He gathered thousands (War: 30,000) to storm Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives; Felix routed them and he escaped.

title: Jews and Syrians fight over citizenship at Caesarea
note: The fight over whether Herod's Caesarea was a Jewish or Greek city reached Nero; his ruling for the Greeks became an immediate cause of the war (2.14.4). Josephus: "under Felix".

title: Porcius Festus succeeds Felix
note: Festus fought the sicarii and an impostor in the wilderness; he heard Paul's appeal to Caesar (Acts 25). Josephus: "'Upon Festus's coming into Judea'".

title: Nero rules for Caesarea's Greeks against its Jews
note: The decision on citizenship rights at Caesarea, Josephus says, 'afforded the grounds of the miseries that followed' and led to war. Josephus: "Burrhus was bribed to obtain the letter".

title: Priests wall off Agrippa II's view; Poppaea wins Nero's consent
note: The priests built a wall to block the king's dining room from seeing into the Temple; Nero let it stand, keeping the high priest Ishmael as hostage. Josephus: "'This was granted them in order to gratify Poppea, Nero's wife, who was a religious woman'".

title: James, "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ", stoned
note: The new high priest Ananus son of Annas, a Sadducee, had James and others stoned; protesting citizens had Agrippa II depose him after three months. The passage is widely accepted as genuine. Josephus: "'Festus was now dead, and Albinus was but upon the road; so he assembled the sanhedrim of judges, and brought before them the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James'".

title: Jesus son of Ananus begins crying “Woe to Jerusalem” at Tabernacles
note: A farmer cried against the city and Temple day and night for seven years and five months. Albinus had him flogged to the bone and released him as a madman. Josephus: "“four years before the war began… came to that feast whereon it is our custom for every one to make tabernacles”". Tabernacles (15–21 Tishri) of AD 62, four years before the war; Albinus's term confirms the year.

title: Josephus sails to Rome at 26; shipwreck and Poppaea
note: Going to free priests Felix had sent to Rome, he survived a shipwreck with about 80 of 600 aboard; through the actor Aliturus he met Poppaea, who freed them. Josephus: "'when I was in the twenty-sixth year of my age, it happened that I took a voyage to Rome'".

title: Agrippa II lets the Levite singers wear linen like the priests
note: Josephus sees this breach of ancestral law as one cause of the coming disaster. Josephus: "'that he might have a memorial of such a novelty'".

title: Herod's Temple finally completed; 18,000 workmen idle
note: To give work to more than 18,000 men, Agrippa had the city paved with white stone. Josephus: "'And now it was that the temple was finished'".

title: Gessius Florus made procurator through Poppaea
note: His wife Cleopatra was a friend of Poppaea; Josephus says Florus's greed drove the Jews to war. Josephus: "'sent as successor to Albinus by Nero'". Josephus calls him the worst procurator, who openly shared in robbers' spoils and 'forced the Jews into the war'.

title: Cestius Gallus visits Jerusalem at Passover; crowds denounce Florus
note: Josephus says three million people appealed to Cestius against Florus, who laughed. Cestius used the Passover lambs to count the pilgrims (6.9.3). Josephus: "“upon the approach of the feast of unleavened bread”". Passover (Nisan) AD 66; some date it to AD 65.

title: The Temple's heavy brass eastern gate opens by itself
note: The gate normally needed twenty men to shut it. The learned took it to mean the Temple's protection was gone. Josephus: "“at the same festival… was seen to be opened of its own accord about the sixth hour of the night”". Same Passover as the light at the altar (AD 66 or 65); Josephus gives the festival and the hour, not the day.

title: Great light shines round the altar at Passover, 8 Xanthicus
note: For half an hour the Temple shone as bright as day. At the same feast a heifer led to sacrifice gave birth to a lamb in the Temple. Josephus: "“on the eighth day of the month Xanthicus, [Nisan,] and at the ninth hour of the night”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date. 'Before the Jews' rebellion' = Passover season AD 66 (some say 65). Ninth hour of the night ≈ 3 a.m. at the end of the night of 8 Nisan.

title: War begins at Caesarea: birds sacrificed at the synagogue on the Sabbath
note: After Nero ruled for the Greeks, a Greek sacrificed birds on an upturned pot at the synagogue entrance on the Sabbath. The fighting that followed was Josephus's formal start of the war. Josephus: "“the war began, in the twelfth year of the reign of Nero, and the seventeenth of the reign of Agrippa, in the month of Artemisius [Jyar]”; “the next day, which was the seventh day of the week”". Artemisius (Iyar) in Nero's 12th year (Oct 65–Oct 66) = spring AD 66; the Sabbath falls in early Iyar. Riots at the Caesarea synagogue and Florus's seizure of Temple money set off the revolt that ended with the Temple's destruction in AD 70.

title: Queen Bernice pleads barefoot before Florus
note: Bernice was in Jerusalem for a Nazirite vow. Florus ignored her, and soldiers killed people in front of her. Josephus: "“about this very time”; she she “stood barefoot before Florus's tribunal, and besought him [to spare the Jews]”". Same days as the massacre of 16 Artemisius, AD 66.

title: Florus plunders the Upper Market; 3,600 killed and Jewish knights crucified
note: After taking 17 talents from the Temple treasury and being mocked, Florus let his troops loose on the Upper Market. He scourged and crucified Jews of equestrian rank, which Josephus calls unprecedented. Josephus: "“This happened upon the sixteenth day of the month Artemisius [Jyar]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date.

title: Chariots and armed troops seen in the clouds, 21 Artemisius
note: Josephus says it would seem a fable if eyewitnesses had not reported it: armies running among the clouds and surrounding cities. Josephus: "“a few days after that feast, on the one and twentieth day of the month Artemisius, [Jyar,]… before sun-setting”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date. Same spring as the Passover portents (AD 66 or 65).

title: Priests hear a voice at Pentecost: “Let us remove hence”
note: The priests felt a quaking, heard a great noise, and then the sound of a multitude saying 'Let us remove hence'. Josephus: "“at that feast which we call Pentecost, as the priests were going by night into the inner [court]”". Pentecost (Sivan) of the same year as the other portents (AD 66 or 65).

title: A star like a sword over the city and a comet for a year
note: The first of the portents Josephus lists. Some identify the comet with Halley's comet of AD 66. Josephus: "“there was a star resembling a sword, which stood over the city, and a comet, that continued a whole year”".

title: Agrippa II's speech urging Jerusalem not to fight Rome
note: Agrippa listed the nations Rome had conquered and warned that war would destroy the city and Temple. The people later drove him out. Josephus: "after Neopolitanus's visit".

title: Rebels seize Masada and kill its Roman garrison
note: The fortress was taken by treachery. Menahem later armed his followers from Herod's armoury there. Josephus: "“at this time it was that some… made an assault upon a certain fortress called Masada”".

title: Sacrifice for Caesar stopped: “the true beginning of our war”
note: The Temple captain Eleazar persuaded the priests to accept no gift or sacrifice from a foreigner, ending the daily offering for the emperor. Josephus: "“this was the true beginning of our war with the Romans; for they rejected the sacrifice of Caesar”".

title: Gentiles of Scythopolis kill their Jewish neighbours (13,000)
note: The Scythopolis Jews had fought for the city against Jewish raiders and were then killed in a grove. Simon son of Saul killed his own family and then himself. Josephus: "after the Caesarea massacre".

title: 50,000 Jews killed at Alexandria under Tiberius Alexander
note: The prefect, himself of Jewish birth, sent two legions into the Jewish quarter. Josephus: "during the same troubles".

title: Damascus massacres its Jews in the gymnasium
note: War 2.20.2 says 10,000 were killed in one hour; Eleazar's Masada speech (7.8.7) says 18,000. Josephus: "“when they were informed of the destruction of the Romans”".

title: Josephus son of Matthias made general of Galilee
note: The Jerusalem assembly named generals for each region; Josephus received both Galilees and Gamala. Josephus: "after the defeat of Cestius".

title: John the Essene appointed general of Thamna, Lydda, Joppa and Emmaus
note: A rare named Essene in public life: a member of the sect commanded rebel forces. Josephus: "“John, the Essene, to the toparchy of Thamna”".

title: Wood-carrying feast: rebels burn the high priest's house and debt archives
note: With the Sicarii, the rebels drove the king's troops from the upper city and burned the houses of Ananias, Agrippa and Bernice and the archives, destroying the records of debts. Josephus: "“the next day was the festival of Xylophory; upon which the custom was for every one to bring wood for the altar”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date. Josephus puts the Xylophory the day before 15 Lous, giving 14 Av (the Mishnah's main wood-offering day is 15 Av).

title: Rebels take the Antonia after a two-day siege and burn it
note: The garrison was killed and the citadel burned. The rebels then besieged Herod's palace. Josephus: "“on the next day, which was the fifteenth of the month Lous, [Ab,] they made an assault upon Antonia… besieged the garrison… two days”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date. The assault began 15 Av; the fall came two days later (≈17 Av).

title: Roman garrison killed on the Sabbath after surrendering under oath
note: Metilius's soldiers gave up their arms on oath and were then killed; only Metilius was spared, after promising to become a Jew. Josephus: "“this murder was perpetrated on the sabbath day”". A Sabbath in Gorpiaeus/Elul AD 66, soon after 7 Elul.

title: 20,000 Jews of Caesarea massacred “on the very same day and hour”
note: Caesarea was emptied of Jews, and Florus sent those who fled to the galleys. Jewish reprisals on Syrian cities led to massacres of Jews across the region. Josephus: "“on the very same day and hour [when the soldiers were slain]”". Same Sabbath as the garrison massacre (Elul AD 66).

title: Menahem's men burn the Roman camp; the garrison flees to Herod's towers
note: Menahem son of Judas the Galilean came from Masada 'in the state of a king'. The king's troops left under terms, and the Romans fled to Hippicus, Phasael and Mariamne. Josephus: "“This was executed on the sixth day of the month Gorpieus [Elul]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date.

title: Former high priest Ananias and his brother Hezekiah killed
note: Ananias's death made Menahem a tyrant. Eleazar's party then killed Menahem in the Temple, and his followers fled to Masada. Josephus: "“on the next day the high priest was caught where he had concealed himself in an aqueduct”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date. 'The next day' after 6 Gorpiaeus = 7 Elul.

title: Jews leave Tabernacles to attack Cestius at Gabao on the Sabbath
note: Cestius burned Lydda, which was empty for the festival. The Jews broke into his ranks near Beth-horon and Gibeon, and Simon bar Giora harried his rear. Josephus: "“the whole multitude were gone up to Jerusalem to the feast of tabernacles”; they fought “without any consideration had of the rest of the seventh day”". A Sabbath during Tabernacles (15–21 Tishri) AD 66; on the lunar reckoning used here, ≈ 18 Tishri = 27 Sep 66.

title: Cestius Gallus enters Jerusalem and burns Bezetha
note: Cestius camped on Scopus for three days, then took the new city and attacked the Temple wall. He withdrew unexpectedly just as Josephus says the city could have fallen. Josephus: "“on the fourth day, which was the thirtieth of the month Hyperbereteus, [Tisri,]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date.

title: Cestius Gallus routed at Beth-horon
note: The retreating 12th Legion lost 5,300 foot and 380 horse and abandoned its siege engines. The victory committed Jerusalem to war. Josephus: "“This defeat happened on the eighth day of the month Dius, [Marchesvan,] in the twelfth year of the reign of Nero”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. On this reckoning AD 66 had no extra Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 17 Mar); if it was intercalated, add ~29 days (hence some put this a month later); a Tyrian solar-calendar reading also gives a later date.

title: Josephus enters Jotapata as Vespasian arrives
note: Vespasian's road-builders cut a way to the city in four days. Josephus's arrival raised the defenders' spirits and Vespasian began the siege. Josephus: "“On the fifth day, which was the twenty-first of the month Artemisius, (Jyar,) Josephus… went into Jotapata”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 67 here follows an intercalated Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 4 Apr); without it, subtract ~29 days.

title: Roman assault on Jotapata repulsed
note: The defenders poured boiling oil on the Romans and spread boiled fenugreek on the boarding planks; six Jews were killed. Josephus: "“This fight happened on the twentieth day of the month Desius [Sivan]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 67 here follows an intercalated Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 4 Apr); without it, subtract ~29 days.

title: Japha falls to Trajan and Titus
note: 15,000 were killed and 2,130 taken captive. Josephus: "“This calamity befell the Galileans on the twenty-fifth day of the month Desius [Sivan.]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 67 here follows an intercalated Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 4 Apr); without it, subtract ~29 days.

title: Cerealis kills 11,600 Samaritans on Mount Gerizim
note: Samaritans who had gathered on their holy mountain were surrounded in the summer heat and killed when they refused to surrender. Josephus: "“This was done on the twenty-seventh day of the month Desius [Sivan]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 67 here follows an intercalated Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 4 Apr); without it, subtract ~29 days.

title: John the Essene killed in the failed attack on Ascalon
note: Niger the Peraite, Silas of Babylon and John the Essene led the attack; Antonius's cavalry routed them twice. Josephus: "“ten thousand men of the Jews' side lay dead, with two of their generals, John and Silas”".

title: Nero appoints Vespasian to command the war
note: Nero, touring Greece, sent Vespasian to Syria. Titus brought the 5th and 10th Legions from Alexandria to join the 15th at Ptolemais. Josephus: "Nero “found no one but Vespasian equal to the task”".

title: Joppa's pirate fleet wrecked by the 'black north wind'
note: A dawn storm smashed the ships on the rocks; 4,200 bodies washed ashore and the Romans razed Joppa again. Josephus: "after Joppa was rebuilt as a pirate base".

title: Placidus takes Mount Tabor
note: Placidus lured the defenders down onto the plain by a feigned retreat. Josephus: "during the siege of Gamala".

title: John of Gischala escapes to Jerusalem after asking for a Sabbath truce
note: Titus granted the Sabbath; John fled in the night. 6,000 of the women and children who followed him were killed. With Gischala, Galilee was subdued. Josephus: "“to grant them leave to celebrate that day, which was the seventh day of the week”".

title: Zealots seize the Temple and choose Phannias as high priest by lot
note: The Zealots took the Temple as their fortress and made a village stonecutter high priest. This was the last high priest. Josephus: "they “cast lots… it fell upon one whose name was Phannias, the son of Samuel, of the village Aphtha”".

title: Jotapata taken on 1 Panemus after a 47-day siege
note: On a deserter's tip the Romans came in at the last watch while the guards slept. About 40,000 died in the siege and the city was razed. Josephus: "“thus was Jotapata taken, in the thirteenth year of the reign of Nero, on the first day of the month Panemus [Tamuz]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 67 here follows an intercalated Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 4 Apr); without it, subtract ~29 days. Josephus's 47 days does not fit exactly between 21 Artemisius and 1 Panemus.

title: Josephus survives the cave lottery, surrenders and foretells Vespasian's rule
note: Of the forty in the cave, Josephus and one other were left after the death lots. He surrendered and told Vespasian he would be emperor, which saved his life. Josephus: "hidden two days in a cave; on the third day betrayed; “Thou, O Vespasian, art Caesar and emperor, thou, and this thy son”". Early Panemus/Tammuz AD 67, two or three days after 1 Panemus.

title: Vespasian returns to Ptolemais, then Caesarea
note: After Jotapata the army went into quarters at Caesarea and Scythopolis. Josephus: "“Vespasian returned to Ptolemais on the fourth day of the month Panemus, [Tamus]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 67 here follows an intercalated Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 4 Apr); without it, subtract ~29 days.

title: Naval battle on the Sea of Galilee after Tarichaeae falls
note: Vespasian's rafts destroyed the rebels' boats; 6,700 died and the lake ran red. (A first-century boat found in 1986 is often linked to this period.) Josephus: "after the fall of Tarichaeae". Late Lous / early Gorpiaeus AD 67, before the selection of prisoners on 8 Gorpiaeus.

title: Vespasian sorts the Tarichaeae prisoners in the Tiberias stadium
note: 1,200 old and weak men were killed, 6,000 young men were sent to Nero to dig the Isthmus canal at Corinth, and 30,400 were sold. Josephus: "“These prisoners were taken on the eighth day of the month Gorpiaeus [Elul]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 67 here follows an intercalated Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 4 Apr); without it, subtract ~29 days.

title: Gamala revolts; Vespasian besieges it
note: Gamala was perched on a camel-shaped ridge. The Romans were thrown back at their first entry, with heavy losses. Josephus: "“the city had first revolted on the four and twentieth day of the month Gorpieus [Elul]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 67 here follows an intercalated Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 4 Apr); without it, subtract ~29 days. Usually read as the start of the siege.

title: Three legionaries undermine a Gamala tower at the morning watch
note: The tower fell with a crash and the defenders panicked. Josephus: "“the men of war sustained the siege till the two and twentieth day of the month Hyperberetmus, [Tisri,]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 67 here follows an intercalated Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 4 Apr); without it, subtract ~29 days.

title: Gamala taken; 4,000 slain and 5,000 leap to their deaths
note: Titus entered by night. A storm wind turned the defenders' missiles back on them, and two women alone survived. Josephus: "“thus was Gamala taken on the three and twentieth day of the month Hyperberetens, [Tisri,]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 67 here follows an intercalated Adar (1 Nisan ≈ 4 Apr); without it, subtract ~29 days.

title: Vespasian enters Gadara, capital of Perea
note: The city's leading men surrendered behind the rebels' backs. Placidus then cleared Perea as far as the Dead Sea. Josephus: "“entered that city on the fourth day of the month Dystrus [Adar]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. Adar of the Jewish year 67/68 = Feb/Mar AD 68.

title: Sicarii from Masada raid Engaddi at Passover; 700 women and children killed
note: The Sicarii fell on Ein Gedi by night during the feast, killed those who could not flee, and carried the harvest back to Masada. Josephus: "“at the feast of unleavened bread, which the Jews celebrate in memory of their deliverance from the Egyptian bondage”". Passover (Nisan) AD 68.

title: Death of Nero, as reported to Vespasian at Caesarea
note: Vespasian halted his advance on Jerusalem. Josephus's 'thirteen years and eight days' should be thirteen years and about eight months. Josephus: "“he was informed that Nero was dead, after he had reigned thirteen years and eight days”". Julian date from Roman sources; Josephus gives the length of the reign.

title: Idumaeans let in during a storm; Ananus and Jesus the high priests killed
note: The Zealots opened the gates under cover of the storm, and 8,500 were killed. Josephus dates the 'beginning of the destruction of the city' from Ananus's death. Josephus: "“there broke out a prodigious storm in the night… amazing concussions and bellowings of the earth”".

title: Zealots murder Zacharias son of Baris (Baruch) in the Temple
note: A sham court of seventy acquitted him, and two Zealots killed him 'in the midst of the temple'. The name is often compared with Matthew 23:35. Josephus: "“they intended to have Zacharias the son of Baruch… slain”".

title: Galba murdered in the Roman Forum; Otho emperor
note: Titus, on his way to greet Galba, turned back on hearing of his death. Josephus: "“Galba was slain in the midst of the Roman market-place”; he ruled “seven months and as many days” (4.9.2)". Julian date from Roman sources.

title: Simon bar Giora admitted into Jerusalem
note: The high priest Matthias son of Boethus and the people invited Simon in against John's Zealots. The city now had three warring factions. Josephus: "“thus did Simon get possession of Jerusalem, in the third year of the war, in the month Xanthicus [Nisan]”". Xanthicus/Nisan, 'third year of the war' = spring AD 69.

title: Otho kills himself after Bedriacum; Vitellius emperor
note: Josephus places the battle 'at Betriacum in Gaul' (actually northern Italy). Josephus: "Otho “slew himself… after he had managed the public affairs three months and two days”". Julian date from Roman sources.

title: Vespasian resumes the campaign from Caesarea
note: He subdued Gophnitica, Acrabattene, Bethel and Ephraim, and rode up to the walls of Jerusalem. Josephus: "“Vespasian removed from Cesarea, on the fifth day of the month Deasius, [Sivan,]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days.

title: The eastern legions proclaim Vespasian emperor
note: Josephus describes the army in Judea forcing the purple on Vespasian, with Tiberius Alexander bringing Egypt in. Vespasian then remembered Josephus's prophecy (4.10.7). Josephus: "the soldiers “declared Vespasian emperor”". Josephus gives no date. Tacitus dates the oath in Alexandria to 1 July 69 (the official dies imperii) and in Judea to 3 July.

title: Vespasian frees Josephus; his chain is cut, not just loosed
note: At Titus's suggestion the chain was cut through, the sign of a man wrongly bound, and Josephus's honour was restored. Josephus: "Vespasian “remember[ed] what Josephus had said to him… so he was much concerned that this man was still in bonds”".

title: Vitellius killed at Rome; 50,000 slain
note: After the Capitol burned, Antonius Primus's army took Rome and Vitellius was dragged out and killed after eight months and five days. Mucianus arrived the next day. Josephus: "“This battle was fought on the third day of the month Apelleus [Casleu]”". Roman sources date Vitellius's death to 20 Dec 69. Josephus's '3 Apellaeus' does not fit the lunar Kislev (≈7 Nov) and is probably his error or a different calendar, so the Roman date is given.

title: Passover AD 70: John's men slip into the inner Temple
note: When Eleazar's party opened the inner court to worshippers, John's men came in with hidden weapons and took it, reducing the factions to two. Josephus: "“on the feast of unleavened bread… the fourteenth day of the month Xanthicus, [Nisan,] when it is believed the Jews were first freed from the Egyptians”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).

title: Titus pitches camp before Jerusalem; the siege begins
note: Titus came with four legions (5th, 10th, 12th, 15th), shutting in Passover pilgrims. Josephus says this crowding caused the famine and the huge death toll. Josephus: "“the fourteenth day of the month Xanthicus, [Nisan,] when the Romans pitched their camp by the city”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug). 5.13.7 gives 14 Xanthicus for the encampment; Titus reached Scopus a few days before.

title: Romans take Jerusalem's first (outer north) wall
note: The battering ram the Jews nicknamed 'Victor' broke through, and the defenders fell back to the second wall. Josephus: "“on the fifteenth day of the siege, which was the seventh day of the month Artemisius, [Jyar,]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).

title: Titus takes the second wall, loses it, and retakes it four days later
note: Titus went in by a narrow breach and was driven out. He took it again and demolished it, leaving the Antonia, Temple and upper city. Josephus: "“Caesar took this wall there on the fifth day after he had taken the first”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug). 'The fifth day after' 7 Artemisius ≈ 12 Iyar (11–12 depending on counting); recaptured about four days later.

title: Banks against the Antonia built 12–29 Artemisius, then burned
note: John of Gischala tunnelled under the banks and set the props alight, and Simon's men burned the other engines. Josephus: "“the Romans began to raise their banks on the twelfth day of the month Artemisius, [Jyar,] so had they much ado to finish them by the twenty-ninth day”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug). The banks were begun 12 Iyar and finished on the 29th (this date); they were destroyed in the days after.

title: Titus builds a wall around the city in three days
note: The wall, 39 furlongs with 13 forts, sealed the city and the famine became extreme. Josephus: "“the whole was completed in three days”". After the banks were lost (end of Iyar), so early Daesius/Sivan AD 70.

title: 115,880 dead carried out through a single gate
note: Mannaeus son of Lazarus reported the count to Titus; deserters said 600,000 poor had been thrown out of the gates. Josephus: "“between the fourteenth day of the month Xanthieus, [Nisan,] when the Romans pitched their camp by the city, and the first day of the month Panemus [Tamuz]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug). The figure covers 14 Nisan to 1 Tammuz; it is dated here at the end of the count.

title: Attack on the Antonia; the undermined wall collapses
note: A Jewish sally against the banks failed. That night John's mine brought the Antonia wall down, but a new inner wall stood behind it. Josephus: "“This attack was made upon the first day of the month Panemus [Tamuz.]”". title: Captured deserters crucified, up to 500 a day
note: Josephus says 'room was wanting for the crosses, and crosses wanting for the bodies'. Josephus: "“they caught every day five hundred Jews; nay, some days they caught more”".

title: Simon bar Giora executes the high priest Matthias and his sons
note: The man who had let Simon in was killed in sight of the Romans with three sons, accused of favouring them. Josephus: "Simon “would not suffer Matthias, by whose means he got possession of the city, to go off without torment”".

title: The Syrian soldier Sabinus dies scaling the Antonia wall
note: Sabinus led eleven men up the new wall and was killed. Josephus: "“These things were done upon the third day of the month Panemus [Tamuz]”". title: Famine: Mary of Bethezob eats her own child
note: Josephus tells it as the worst horror of the famine, recalling the curses of Deuteronomy 28:56–57. It hardened Titus's resolve. Josephus: "“There was a certain woman that dwelt beyond Jordan, her name was Mary”".

title: Jesus son of Ananus killed by a siege stone, still crying “Woe”
note: On the wall he cried 'Woe to me also' and was killed by a stone from a Roman engine. Josephus: "after “seven years and five months”: “Woe, woe to myself also!”".

title: John of Gischala gives himself up from the tunnels
note: John, starved out, surrendered and was sentenced to life imprisonment; 2,000 dead were found in the tunnels. Josephus: "“As for John, he wanted food, together with his brethren, in these caverns, and begged that the Romans would now give him their right hand”; “John condemned to perpetual imprisonment”".

title: Simon bar Giora rises from the ground in white and purple on the Temple site
note: After failing to tunnel out, Simon tried to frighten the guards. He was chained and kept for the triumph. Josephus: "Simon “put on a white frock… and appeared out of the ground in the place where the temple had formerly been”".

title: Antioch: the apostate Antiochus accuses the Jews and the Sabbath is suppressed
note: A renegade Jew accused his people of plotting to burn the city, which led to killings and a ban on Sabbath rest. After a real fire (AD 70/71) Titus refused to expel the Jews. Josephus: "Antiochus was “not permitting them to rest on the seventh day”".

title: Romans take the Antonia by night
note: Twelve men crept up, killed the sleeping guards and sounded a trumpet. The garrison fled and the Romans fought into the Temple court until driven back. Josephus: "“two days afterward… about the ninth hour of the night, through the ruins, to the tower of Antonia”". 'Two days after' 3 Panemus ≈ 5 Tammuz, during the night (ninth hour).

title: Daily sacrifice ceases on 17 Panemus
note: The daily sacrifice stopped for lack of men to offer it, and Titus sent Josephus to plead with John. Rabbinic tradition (m. Taanit 4:6) also puts its end on 17 Tammuz, the fast day. Josephus: "“on that very day, which was the seventeenth day of Panemus, [Tamuz,] the sacrifice called the Daily Sacrifice had failed”". title: Temple cloisters by the Antonia set on fire
note: The Jews burned the cloister joining the Antonia, which Josephus calls the beginning of the burning of the sanctuary; the Romans burned the next cloister on the 24th. Josephus: "“they set the north-west cloister… on fire… two days after which, or on the twenty-fourth day of the forenamed month, the Romans set fire to the cloister that joined to the other”". Jews' fire ≈ 22 Tammuz; Roman fire 24 Tammuz (≈ 22 Jul 70).

title: Jews trap Roman soldiers in the burning western cloister
note: The defenders filled the roof of the western cloister with wood, bitumen and pitch and pretended to retreat. Many Romans who climbed it died in the fire. Josephus: "“on the twenty-seventh day of the forenamed month [Panemus or Tamuz] contrived such a stratagem”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. title: Roman standards set up in the Temple court; Titus hailed imperator
note: The legions sacrificed to their standards in the Temple court. Loot was so plentiful that gold sold in Syria at half its value. Josephus: "“brought their ensigns to the temple and set them over against its eastern gate; and there did they offer sacrifices to them”". Immediately after the Temple burned (10 Lous), Av AD 70.

title: Titus parleys with Simon and John at the Xystus bridge
note: The tyrants asked to leave with their families for the desert. Titus refused and ordered the city burned and plundered. Josephus: "“he placed himself on the western side of the outer [court of the] temple… above the Xystus”". Av AD 70, shortly after the Temple fell.

title: Lower city burned as far as Siloam
note: The archives, the council house and the Ophel quarter were burned; the rebels held only the upper city. Josephus: "“the Romans drove the robbers out of the lower city, and set all on fire as far as Siloam”". Av AD 70.

title: Priests hand over Temple treasures to Titus
note: Jesus son of Thebuthi gave up two candlesticks, tables, bowls and the priestly vestments; the treasurer Phineas surrendered the priests' garments and spices. Josephus: "“one of the priests, the son of Thebuthus, whose name was Jesus”". Between 20 Lous and 7 Gorpiaeus AD 70.

title: Banks completed against the Temple; Titus orders the gates set on fire
note: The rams failed against the Temple walls, so the gates were burned. The next day Titus's council argued over whether to spare the sanctuary. Josephus: "“two of the legions had completed their banks on the eighth day of the month Lous [Ab]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. title: Titus begins banks against the upper city
note: Timber had to be brought from 100 furlongs away. The Idumaeans tried to negotiate a surrender. Josephus: "“this on the twentieth day of the month Lous [Ab]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days.
