title: Josephus's totals: 97,000 captives and 1,100,000 dead
note: He explains the numbers by the Passover crowds. A census by paschal lambs under Cestius had counted 256,500 sacrifices, about 2.7 million people. Josephus: "“the number of those that were carried captive during this whole war was… ninety-seven thousand… those that perished during the whole siege eleven hundred thousand”". Summary given after the fall (Gorpiaeus/Elul AD 70).

title: Titus orders the city and Temple razed; three towers and the west wall left
note: The rest was levelled so that visitors would not believe it had been inhabited. The 10th Legion stayed as the garrison. Josephus: "“Caesar gave orders that they should now demolish the entire city and temple, but… leave… Phasaelus, and Hippicus, and Mariamne”". Right after the capture, Gorpiaeus/Elul AD 70.

title: Banks finished and the upper city wall breached
note: The rebels lost heart, left the towers of Hippicus, Phasael and Mariamne, and fled into the valley under Siloam and the tunnels. Josephus: "“now were the banks finished on the seventh day of the month Gorpieus, [Elul,] in eighteen days' time”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).

title: Jerusalem taken on 8 Gorpiaeus
note: The whole city was taken and burned. Josephus says it had been taken five times before and desolated twice, 2,177 years after its founding by Melchizedek and 1,179 years after David. Josephus: "“thus was Jerusalem taken, in the second year of the reign of Vespasian, on the eighth day of the month Gorpeius [Elul]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. AD 70 here: 1 Nisan ≈ 2 Apr, consistent with the app's 10 Av ≈ early August; scholars who intercalate 69/70 differently put these dates ~a month later (10 Av ≈ 29/30 Aug).

title: Titus marks Domitian's birthday at Caesarea; 2,500 captives killed
note: Captives were killed fighting beasts, burned and made to fight each other. Josephus: "“he solemnized the birthday of his brother Domitian after a splendid manner”". Josephus gives no date. Domitian's birthday was 24 October (Suetonius), so 24 Oct 70.

title: Titus marks Vespasian's birthday at Berytus with more captive deaths
note: There were more shows and many more captives died. Josephus: "“exhibited a still more pompous solemnity about his father's birthday”". Josephus gives no date. Vespasian's birthday was 17 November (Suetonius), so 17 Nov 70.

title: Triumph of Vespasian and Titus in Rome; Simon bar Giora executed
note: The Temple spoils were carried, including the golden table, the lampstand and a copy of the Law. Simon was dragged to the Forum and executed. Josephus: "the procession ending “at the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus”".

title: Temple tax diverted to Jupiter Capitolinus; veterans settled at Emmaus
note: Vespasian kept Judea as his own property, settled 800 veterans at Emmaus (Motza), and imposed the Jewish tax (fiscus Judaicus). Josephus: "“enjoined every one of them to bring two drachmae every year into the Capitol”".

title: Lucilius Bassus takes Herodium
note: This began the mopping-up of the last rebel strongholds. Josephus: "Bassus “took that citadel which was in Herodium”".

title: Vespasian gives Josephus his house, citizenship and a pension
note: Josephus lived in Vespasian's old house and received lands in Judea; he wrote his histories there. Josephus: "'when we were come to Rome ... he gave me an apartment in his own house ... honored me with the privilege of a Roman citizen'".

title: Machaerus surrenders to save the young Eleazar from crucifixion
note: After the captured Eleazar was scourged and a cross set up in sight of the walls, the garrison gave up the fortress in exchange for his life. The Romans then killed the 'strangers' in the lower town. Josephus: "Bassus “resolved to besiege it, by filling up the valley that lay on the east side”".

title: Bassus destroys 3,000 fugitives in the forest of Jardes
note: Fugitives from Jerusalem and Machaerus were surrounded and killed, including Judas son of Ari. Josephus: "“he marched hastily to the forest of Jarden, as it is called”".

title: Antiochus IV of Commagene deposed (fourth year of Vespasian)
note: Caesennius Paetus accused him of plotting with Parthia; his kingdom was annexed. Josephus: "“in the fourth year of the reign of Vespasian”".

title: The Alans invade Media and Armenia
note: The Alans came through the Caspian Gates, plundered Media and nearly lassoed King Tiridates of Armenia. Josephus: "“This nation about this time laid a design of falling upon Media”".

title: Flavius Silva besieges Masada
note: Silva walled Masada round and built a ramp on the White Promontory against Eleazar son of Jair's Sicarii. Josephus: "“Flavius Silva succeeded him as procurator… made an expedition against it”".

title: Masada falls: 960 die by their own hands, 15 Xanthicus
note: After Eleazar's speeches the defenders killed their families and then each other, and burned everything but the food. Two women and five children hid and survived. Josephus: "“This calamitous slaughter was made on the fifteenth day of the month Xanthicus [Nisan]”". Josephus's Macedonian month read as the Jewish lunar month (his own equation); computed from the astronomical new moon, day 1 = daylight after first crescent, Nisan = month whose 14th falls on/after the spring equinox; ±1–2 days. The year is disputed: AD 73 is traditional, AD 74 is favoured by many since inscriptions show Silva governing into 73/74. AD 74 gives ≈ 1 Apr 74 on this reckoning; other calendar readings (e.g. Tyrian) put it some weeks later.

title: Sicarii fugitives in Alexandria handed over; they refuse to call Caesar lord
note: The Jewish elders handed over 600 Sicarii. Under torture none would call Caesar lord, which Josephus admired. Josephus: "“not one of these children was so far overcome by these torments, as to name Caesar for their lord”".

title: Vespasian has the temple of Onias in Egypt closed
note: Lupus and then Paulinus took the offerings, shut the gates and stopped all worship there. Josephus: "“the duration of the time from the building of this temple till it was shut up again was three hundred and forty-three years”".

title: Jonathan the weaver leads a desert movement in Cyrene
note: Jonathan promised signs in the desert, and the governor Catullus crushed them. Catullus then killed 3,000 wealthy Jews, and Jonathan falsely accused Josephus in Rome. Josephus: "“one Jonathan, a vile person, and by trade a weaver”".

title: Vespasian's Temple of Peace receives the Temple's gold vessels
note: The Law and the purple veils of the sanctuary were kept in the palace. Josephus: "“he also laid up therein those golden vessels and instruments that were taken out of the Jewish temple”".

title: Josephus presents the Jewish War to Vespasian and Titus
note: Agrippa II wrote 62 letters vouching for it; Titus ordered it published. Josephus: "'Titus was so desirous that the knowledge of these affairs should be taken from these books alone, that he subscribed his own hand to them'".

title: Josephus writes about Jesus in the Antiquities (Testimonium Flavianum)
note: Josephus calls Jesus a wise man and doer of wonderful works, condemned by Pilate at the urging of leading men, and says 'the tribe of Christians, so named from him, are not extinct at this day'. Josephus: "'Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man ... Pilate ... had condemned him to the cross'".

title: Josephus completes the Antiquities in Domitian's 13th year
note: Twenty books of Jewish history from Creation to the eve of the war; the Life was added as an appendix. Josephus: "'which is the thirteenth year of the reign of Caesar Domitian, and the fifty-sixth year of my own life'".

title: Against Apion names 22 sacred books, prophecy ending with Artaxerxes
note: Five books of Moses, thirteen of the prophets and four of hymns and precepts; books after Artaxerxes were not trusted equally because 'there hath not been an exact succession of prophets'. The earliest Jewish list of the canon. Josephus: "'only twenty-two books, which contain the records of all the past times'".
